1:
The opening formula explains what follows. Gill takes the note that there was no king in Israel to mark the period between Joshua's death and the judges, set down to account for wickedness committed with impunity, the adultery, sodomy and murder afterwards related. Keil dates the events from an independent detail, that Phinehas was high priest at the time according to the next chapter, so that the account belongs to the years immediately after Joshua's death; and he sets out the shape of the whole: this chapter the crime at Gibeah which occasioned the war, the next the war, the last what the congregation did to preserve Benjamin. He notes too that the Levite sojourned, meaning he lived outside a Levitical town. Ellicott observes that four whole months is literally days, four months, which some make a year and four months, though he judges the point bears little on the story.

What the woman actually did is the chapter's first question, and the commentators divide sharply. Clarke assembles the ancient witnesses and finds them unanimous against the English: neither the Latin, the Greek, the Targum nor Josephus takes the word to imply conjugal infidelity, the first saying she left him, the second that she was angry, the Targum that she despised him, Josephus that she was alienated. He adds Houbigant's rendering to the same effect, and concludes that they had contentions, that she ceased to love him, and that she went home to her father. Gill reports the same alternatives, the Targum's despised and Kimchi and Ben Gersom's turning aside to her father's house, and supplies the argument that clinches it for him: had she been guilty of such a crime, her husband would never have sought to reconcile her and take her again, since by the law of God she deserved not merely to be put away but to be put to death. Clarke reasons the same way, that a man would hardly follow an adulteress to speak to her heart. Keil renders the clause without comment and reads the following verb as bringing back her heart, dismissing the alternative pointing as a needless conjecture.

Henry takes the harder reading and builds on it. He treats the elopement as adultery, notes that the Chaldee reads only that she carried herself insolently, and infers from her going unprosecuted that there was no judge in Israel, since otherwise she would have been put to death. His complaint is against the father rather than the daughter: had her husband turned her out unjustly, her father ought to have pitied her, but when she departed treacherously he ought not to have countenanced her sin, and perhaps she would not have violated her duty had she not known too well where she would be kindly received. Children's ruin, he adds, is often owing very much to parents' indulgence. He quotes Bishop Hall's observation that there is no complaint of a disordered state but a Levite stands at one end of it, agent in Micah's idolatry and patient in the wickedness of Gibeah, and remarks that in all this book no others of that tribe are mentioned.

The errand itself everyone reads kindly. Ellicott glosses the idiom as speaking to her heart, bringing about a kindly reconciliation, and notes that the couple of asses implies one was to carry the wife back. Henry makes the point of law behind the gesture, that had the husband put her away it would have been a crime to return to her, but since she had gone of herself it was a virtue to forgive; and he takes the phrase to imply she was already in sorrow, comparing the promise to bring adulterous Israel into the wilderness and speak comfortably to her. Clarke reads the father's gladness as hope of completely reconciling his daughter and her husband; Gill notes only that the husband arose from where he lived.
4:
Why the father kept pressing is answered twice, and the second answer is grim. Ellicott allows first the full rights of hospitality, which are in the East so specially sacred, and a wish to win back the Levite's heart to his erring daughter. At the third detention he supplies another: considering the remorselessly savage revenge still permitted to an Eastern husband in punishment of unfaithfulness, the father might well desire to be thoroughly assured that the Levite was not dissembling and intended no sanguinary retribution once he had her away. Gill keeps to the surface: the father-in-law prevailed on him to stay, and on the fourth day the agreed period was up.

The father's repeated formula is a Hebrew idiom the commentators enjoy. Ellicott renders it literally as prop up thy heart and compares the Latin idiom; Keil notes that the imperative form is unusual. The second, rendered tarry until afternoon, they take as another imperative: Keil gives tarry till the day turns, that is, till midday is past, and Ellicott agrees, noting that the Greek, Chaldee and Latin versions all take it so. Clarke gives no grammar but a reason, that they tarried merely to avoid the heat of the day, very inconvenient in travelling; Ellicott notes that except in winter most journeys are made early or late for the same cause.

The third formula produces a flat contradiction. Clarke translates the phrase rendered the day groweth to an end as the day is about to pitch its tent, near the hour when travellers ordinarily pitched their tents for the night. Ellicott rejects exactly this: it is literally the bending or declining of the day, and not, as the margin of our version has it, the pitching time of the day. Keil supports him without naming the dispute, taking the word as the infinitive of a root meaning to bend. Ellicott lingers on one more literalism, that home is to thy tent, which he thinks may be more than a mere reminiscence of the earlier stage of the national existence.

Keil takes the opportunity for two textual notes. He defends the received form of the verb for the Levite turning back as quite in place and not to be altered on the authority of the Greek version and one Hebrew codex; and he explains the interchange of plural and singular in the father's last appeal from the fact that the party departing was plural while the decision rested with the man alone. Ellicott reads the same appeal psychologically: the father had purposely detained him till late in hopes of another night under his roof, and the forms of Eastern politeness made resistance difficult.

Ellicott alone draws a character from the delay, and he divides the blame. The Levite, he says, is conscious that if the father has been too pressing he has himself been too self-indulgent and too fond of good living; his experience is that of all weak and vacillating people, first unnecessary delay and then overstrained hurry. Keil records the outcome without comment: the Levite would remain no longer but set out and came with his companions to before Jebus, that is Jerusalem, only two hours from Bethlehem. Gill marks the same movement plainly, that they rose from table having comfortably refreshed themselves.
10:
The refusal to lodge in Jebus is treated as the hinge of the disaster. Keil records that when the day had gone far down the attendant proposed turning aside into the Jebusite city, but his master was unwilling to enter a city of foreigners where there were none of the sons of Israel, and would push on to Gibeah or Ramah. Gill follows the Targum in glossing the phrase as a city of the children of the Gentiles, and reads the refusal as a testimonial: by this it appears the Levite was a good man, shunning all appearance of evil and the company of wicked men, as became his profession. He adds a difficulty of his own, that he would surely not have called it so had it been inhabited even in part by Judah and Benjamin. Clarke supplies the history behind that: Jerusalem was partly conquered by Judah after Joshua's death, but the Jebusites kept the stronghold of Zion until David expelled them. Ellicott turns the same fact into a date, arguing that their complete and undisturbed possession here shows the narrative falls early.

Ellicott times the journey closely and blames the delay for what follows. Jerusalem, he notes, is two hours from Bethlehem, so the travellers reached it about five o'clock, and the father, by his unwise neglect to speed the parting guest, had greatly added to the perils of their journey in a half-conquered country and such wild times. Gibeah he identifies as the Gibeah of Saul where the first king was born, one of the fourteen cities of Benjamin and the modern Tuleil el Ful, four miles further on Josephus' reckoning; Ramah he places two miles beyond, the two towns being often named together. The sun went down on them because they were evidently reluctant to stop at Gibeah, though it was dangerous to travel after dark and the Palestinian twilight is very brief; and the phrase which belongeth to Benjamin he explains by the existence of many other Gibeahs. Keil gives the same route without the clock.

One suggestion of Ellicott's turns the choice from piety into miscalculation. The Levite is naturally anxious to push homewards, but perhaps, he says, he knew Gibeah did not bear a good character and thought it better to reach Ramah if possible, since where there are no public inns each town gets a character of its own from travellers' reports. Gill sees only that they turned out of their road instead of passing by, and Keil that they turned aside to pass the night there.

What met them is measured against a standard the commentators take for granted. Ellicott corrects the rendering first: not a street but the open place, the square or market-place, often a space outside the walls, and he cites Job's boast that the stranger did not lodge in the street. He then presses the point: the angels at Sodom would have met the same neglect but for Lot, and this failure of the very first duty of the East was sufficient at once to prove the base condition into which Gibeah had fallen. Keil records the fact flatly, that the Levite remained in the market-place of the town because no one received them into his house. Clarke disputes the premise Ellicott builds on. There was probably no inn at this place, he grants, so lodging could come only by hospitality; but to say there were no inns in those primitive times is not true, since Joseph's brethren loosed their sacks at an inn, the house of Rahab was an inn, and the woman whose house Samson frequented at Gaza kept a place of public entertainment.
16:
Every detail of the old man's introduction is read as significant. Keil notes that he was of the mountains of Ephraim and dwelt as a stranger in Gibeah, whose inhabitants were Benjaminites, a fact set down here as a preliminary introduction to what follows. Henry builds four points on the verse. The rescuer was a sojourner, and one who was himself a sojourner knew the heart of a stranger; of all the tribes the Benjamites had most reason to be kind to travellers, their ancestor having been born on the road near this place, yet they were hard-hearted where an Ephraimite had compassion. He was old, retaining some of the expiring virtue of an Israelite, for the rising generation was entirely corrupted and what good remained was only with those going off. And he came home from the field at eventide, seemingly the only labourer that evening brought home to Gibeah, the rest given up to sloth, so that no marvel there was among them, as in Sodom, abundance of uncleanness where there was abundance of idleness. Gill notes only that though in years and of some substance he still attended his calling.

Henry pauses over what did not happen. It was strange, he says, that those who designed so ill when it was dark did not feign kindness and invite the travellers in, gaining a fairer opportunity for their villainy; either they had not wit enough to be so designing, or not wickedness enough to be so deceiving. Perhaps, he adds, none thought of it separately until in the dark they got together to contrive what mischief they should do, for bad people in confederacy make one another much worse than any would be alone. On the welcome he observes that the old man did not wait to be asked but anticipated them, a charitable disposition expecting only opportunity and not importunity, and credited the Levite's account unquestioned, since charity is not apt to distrust but hopeth all things.

One clause of the Levite's answer is disputed. Keil renders it I walk at the house of Jehovah, and no one receives me into his house, and argues against the common rendering that he was going to the house of the Lord, since the verb with this preposition never means going to a place, for which the simple accusative serves; it means going through a place, or going with. Henry takes the disputed sense as settled and reasons from it, supposing the Levite meant to attend there with a trespass offering for his family's sins or a peace offering for its mercies, and suggesting that had the men of Gibeah known his destination they might have been the less willing to entertain him, as the Samaritans would not receive Christ because his face was toward Jerusalem.

The hospitality is described in domestic detail. Ellicott observes that the Levite asked only shelter, providing for his own wants, and that thy servants is ordinary Eastern obsequiousness. Clarke explains the provender: in pastoral countries there was no hay, but they took great care of their straw, chopped it very small, mixed it with barley, beans or pounded date kernels, made it into balls and fed their cattle with it, much as chaff is used in England. He paraphrases the old man's reply as a refusal of the offer: keep your bread and wine and your straw, since you may need them before your journey ends, and I will supply all your wants. Ellicott and Keil agree that the greeting of peace is here an assurance of help rather than a salutation, Keil glossing the next words as let me provide for them. Ellicott notes two customs, the humane Eastern practice of attending first to the animals, and foot-washing as a first necessity after travel in hot countries where only sandals are worn. Keil records that the host mixed the fodder himself.
22:
The phrase naming the attackers is itself contested. Ellicott states flatly that only by a deeply-rooted misconception is the word capitalised: it is no name of an evil spirit but an ordinary noun, so that the phrase means sons of worthlessness, worthless fellows, and only later became a kind of proper name. Henry takes it in precisely the sense Ellicott rejects, glossing it as ungovernable men who would endure no yoke, children of the devil, for he is Belial, joining him in rebellion against God's government. Clarke keeps to abuse rather than etymology, calling them profligate fellows and genuine sodomites in practice, worse than brutes, a compound of beast and devil inseparably blended. Keil settles only the grammar, the construct state treating it as one idea.

The Sodom parallel is drawn by everyone, hardest by Henry. Keil observes that the demand was the very same the Sodomites made of Lot, and that the verb for beating at the door indicates gradual increase; Ellicott notes the same rising noise and the close resemblance to that hideous narrative. Henry adds a geographical aggravation, that the Dead Sea, the standing monument of God's vengeance on Sodom, bounded Canaan not many miles off, so that the men had seen it many a time and would not take warning, but did worse than Sodom. He quotes Bishop Hall asking who would have expected such abomination from the loins of Jacob, when even the worst pagans were saints to them, and what it availed them to have the ark in Shiloh with Sodom in their streets, God's law in their fringes but the devil in their hearts. He asks why fire did not fall as at Sodom, and answers that God left the punishment to Israel's sword and reserved his own for the future state.

Ellicott follows the story forward instead of backward. The horror it excited, he says, lasted for centuries, and he cites the prophet twice, that they have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah, and that Israel has sinned from the days of Gibeah. He quotes Milton on the sons of Belial who wander forth flown with insolence and wine, with the streets of Sodom and that night in Gibeah for witness; and he charges Josephus with dishonestly suppressing the darkest features of the story.

The word the host uses draws a note on rhetoric. Ellicott insists it is from no deficiency of moral indignation that so mild a term as folly is chosen, since a crime too dark for ordinary reproach is more deeply expressed by a word the hearer corrects for himself; he compares Virgil calling a cannibal tyrant merely unpraised. Keil notes that the term denotes shameful licentiousness, the masculine standing as the more general gender.

On the offer the host then makes, they part company. Clarke refuses all mitigation: Lot made the same proposal, but nothing can excuse either, and though the rights of hospitality were sacred in the East and a man would defend his guest at the cost of his life, how a father could make such a proposal about his virgin daughter must remain among the things that are incomprehensible. Henry grants the principle and pleads circumstances: the host had no power to prostitute his daughter and ought not to have done evil that good might come, yet the proposal may be in part excused by his terror, his concern for his guests, and too close a regard to Lot's example, especially as he did not find that the angels reproved Lot; and perhaps he hoped it would send them back to their common harlots. Keil says only that the old man sought, like Lot, to defend his guests by the sacred rights of hospitality. Gill reports the scene plainly, that they were making their hearts merry with wine after supper and talking of their country and friends when the door was beaten.
25:
Clarke fixes the responsibility by way of a verb. The word rendered simply took, he says, means rather to seize by violence: the woman would not go out, and her husband forced her out to save his own body, which shows how little he loved her and explains their earlier separation. He then condemns all three together — the men of Gibeah, the Levite who saved his own body at the expense of his wife's modesty, reputation and life, and the old man who would have saved his guest at the expense of his daughter — as characters that humanity and modesty wish buried in everlasting oblivion. Gill adds only a bleak guess about why the daughter was refused, that the men knew her and had no affection for her, perhaps because she was not handsome enough for them.

On the night itself Clarke registers that the English is too gentle: the familiar rendering is a modest translation that does not carry the original, since the intensive form of the Hebrew verb designates the frequency of the act, and he gives the fuller sense only in Latin, remarking that even the Arabic version is not too strong. Of the dismissal at first light he observes that their turpitude could not bear the full light of day.

What happened at the door is described the same way by all of them and named by only some. Keil records that at first dawn she fell before the door of the house in which her lord was and lay till sunrise; that her husband found her when he opened the door to go his way, having given up all thought of recovering her from the barbarous crowd; that she lay with her hands upon the threshold, meaning with outstretched arms; and that she gave no answer, having died of the night's ill-treatment. Clarke states it more starkly, that she had strength to reach the door but not to knock, and when she reached it she fell down dead. Ellicott reads the posture rather than the fact, taking the hands upon the threshold as stretched toward her husband in one last agony of appeal, and citing the Latin that has them scattered there. Gill assumes the husband had lain awake, thinking it scarcely reasonable that he should sleep quietly after such a riot, and takes his morning words as spoken on the supposition that she slept.

Ellicott is the only one to comment on how the story is told, and he does it twice. Of the woman's return he says it would be scarcely possible to enhance the pathos and horror the sacred writer throws into these simple words. Of the words after the husband's command he observes that the writer, in his horror, will not say she was dead; and he corrects the article in the next clause, that it is not an ass but the ass, the one which had borne her living. The omission of every detail, he concludes, and the narration of the naked facts in the simplest words, with not a word about the Levite's feelings or the old man's, is a striking example of the difference between the ancient and modern historic method.

Ellicott alone attempts a reckoning of desert, and it falls on more than the townsmen. If punishment came to the wretched woman in the guise of her sin, the prime cause of the whole catastrophe, then the Levite was punished both for condoning an offence which could not be condoned and for the unmanly cowardice or heartless self-absorption which alone could have let him accept personal safety at such a price. Keil records the aftermath without judgement, that the man took the corpse upon his ass to carry it home.
29:
The dismemberment is described as a procedure and read as a summons. Keil renders it as cutting the body up according to its bones, as slaughtered animals are cut in pieces, and says the twelve pieces were sent into the whole territory of Israel, that is to all twelve tribes, in the expectation that everyone who saw would say no such thing had happened since Israel came up out of Egypt. He glosses the closing imperative as make up your minds and say on, that is, decide how this unparalleled wickedness is to be punished, and calls the sending of the pieces a symbolical act. Ellicott gives the same literal phrase, according to her bone, and settles the arithmetic: one piece for each tribe, Benjamin probably appealed to with the rest, and no need to suppose one was sent to eastern Manasseh or to Levi. Gill adds from Josephus that the messengers were commanded to declare what the cause of her death had been.

Both Clarke and Ellicott reach independently for the same modern parallel. Clarke has no doubt a circumstantial account of the barbarity went with each piece, and thinks the pieces themselves were understood as an execration: if the tribes would not avenge his wrongs, they might be hewn in pieces like the murdered woman. He then describes a Highland custom, that when one clan wished to call the rest to avenge its wrongs it took a wooden cross, dipped it in blood, and sent it by a special messenger through all the clans; it was called the fire cross because at sight of it each clan lighted a beacon, giving notice that a general rising was immediately to take place. Ellicott says the narrative takes us back to wild times, when the passions of men expressed themselves in wild and fierce expedients, and cites three analogues: the pieces of an ox sent round by Saul, the same practice among the ancient Scythians on Lucian's report, and many such customs among the Highlanders, repeated even in recent days among the Arab tribes.

On the effect the two agree and describe it differently. Clarke says they were all struck with the enormity of the crime and held it a sovereign disgrace to all the tribes, renders the summons literally as put it to yourselves, take counsel upon it, and speak, and marks it as the prelude to the council of the next chapter. Ellicott reads it as vindicating the Levite's judgement, the verse showing he had successfully gauged the depths of moral indignation still lying in his countrymen's hearts; the story thrilled through all Palestine and awoke a determined desire for retribution on the guilty inhabitants of Gibeah, and the whole nation felt the stain and the shame. Gill notes only that those who saw the pieces were also made acquainted with the cause.

Clarke closes the chapter by explaining what he has not done. He has passed over its abominable transactions as lightly as he could, and will make no apology to the learned or unlearned reader for leaving some things untranslated. Then he draws his lesson: what a blessing are wholesome laws, and a vigorous and attentive magistracy. These wretched people had no form of government and every one did what was right in his own eyes, their own eye, that is their corrupt inclination, being the measure and rule of their conduct; and how bad a rule that is, the abuse and murder of the Levite's wife testify. He ends by telling the reader to bless God for a civil government.
